extracted.intended_audience: policy analysts, regulated parties, researchers, and public commenters searching Federal Register for regulatory impact analyses and related supporting documents
extracted.subtask_description: Locate and review Federal Register entries and dockets that reference or include Regulatory Impact Analyses (RIAs), Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analyses (IRFAs), and related economic, environmental, and paperwork analyses. Useful for preparing comments, conducting policy review, or verifying agency compliance with executive orders and statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 12866 & 13563 cost‑benefit requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 direct agencies to assess all costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if regulation is necessary, to select regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits (including potential economic, environmental, public health and safety effects, distributive impacts, and equity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must examine the impact of rulemakings as required by these EOs; language appears repeatedly asking agencies to assess costs/benefits and choose approaches that maximize net benefits. Used as the primary framing for preparing a Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA).

rubrics_metrics.name: RIA requirement for major/economically significant rules (>$100 million)
rubrics_metrics.description: A regulatory impact analysis must be prepared for major rules with effects of $100 million or more in any one year (economically significant actions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pages repeatedly state that OIRA designates actions as 'significant' or 'economically significant' under EO 12866 and that an RIA is required for such actions; agencies summarize the RIA in the Federal Register and provide full analyses in the docket or at regulations.gov.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) analysis requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Regulatory Flexibility Act requires an agency to prepare a regulatory flexibility analysis for rules unless the agency certifies that the rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency texts specify when the RFA applies, note certification when no significant impact is expected, and identify conformity requirements (e.g., section 604). Some notices explain the RFA's scope and its application to small rural hospitals or other defined groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (IRFA) inclusion and summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Where applicable, agencies prepare an Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (IRFA) as part of the rulemaking record and may summarize costs and benefits in the preamble (e.g., 'Preliminary Regulatory Impact Analysis/Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (PRIA)').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show agencies publishing PRIA/IRFA titles, listing them in the reference section, and correcting records when preliminary estimates differ from those in the PRIA; dockets on regulations.gov typically host the full IRFA/PRIA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA)/OMB review and significance designation
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA/OMB reviews rules designated as 'significant regulatory action' and may determine an action is economically significant (triggering additional review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preambles note that OIRA has reviewed or designated the proposed/final rule as significant under EO 12866; this triggers RIA preparation and often additional documentation and interagency review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) analysis and OMB paperwork review
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must address Paperwork Reduction Act requirements when rules create information collection or third‑party disclosure burdens; OMB review under the PRA may be required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notices state whether third-party disclosure requirements exist and whether PRA/OIRA review is needed; some items point readers to the PRA analysis in the proposed rule or docket.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (UMRA) analysis requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: When applicable, an Unfunded Mandates Reform Act analysis must be prepared to assess federal mandates and their effects (e.g., threshold analyses for mandates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several entries reference UMRA analyses alongside PRIA/IRFA and other supporting documents; agencies include UMRA analysis in the docket when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: NEPA/environmental impact analysis coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must determine whether an action individually or cumulatively has a significant effect on the human environment and whether an Environmental Assessment (EA) or Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) is required (e.g., citing 21 CFR 25.30(h)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preambles sometimes state a NEPA determination (no significant effect) and explain that no EA/EIS is required; RIAs are referenced alongside environmental analyses when preparing the supporting record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of the RIA/PRIA in the administrative record/docket (e.g., regulations.gov)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Regulatory Impact Analysis (and related documents like PRIA, IRFA) must be made available as supporting documents in the administrative record and commonly are posted at regulations.gov or the agency docket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many excerpts explicitly tell readers where to find the full RIA (regulations.gov, specific docket numbers, agency economic staff webpages) and note when corrections or additions have been made to the administrative record to reflect updated estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of Need in RIA/notice
rubrics_metrics.description: An RIA or notice should include a 'Statement of Need' that explains why the regulatory action is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some notices explicitly state that the RIA section begins with a 'Statement of Need' to ensure that the impacts of the notice/rule are fully understood; this frames subsequent cost/benefit and alternatives analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost and benefit estimation methodology and data sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: RIAs must present estimates of costs and benefits, including the methodology and data sources used to derive those estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excerpts reference agencies using consistent methodologies and data sources (and pointing to earlier RIAs for detailed discussion); commenters sometimes challenge the evidence or estimates, prompting agencies to justify methods and data in responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory or sector‑specific RIA triggers and conformity requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain statutes or provisions (e.g., section 1102(b) relating to small rural hospitals, other named statutes) impose additional RIA or analysis requirements or define scope for which analysis must conform to specific statutory sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies identify when statutory triggers require RIA preparation (and define affected entities such as small rural hospitals), and note how analyses must conform to statutory provisions (e.g., section 604 of the RFA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency determination and certification of non‑significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may determine and certify that a rule is not a 'significant regulatory action' under EO 12866 or that the rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities, thereby obviating a full RIA/RFA analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several notices include boilerplate language certifying no significant economic impact or that the action is not significant under EO 12866; such determinations are documented in the preamble and explain why a full RIA is not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline selection guidance (e.g., pre‑statute baseline)
rubrics_metrics.description: When statutory or practical constraints affect what would have occurred otherwise, agencies may specify the baseline used for estimating impacts (for example, using a 'pre‑statute baseline' when a moratorium prevents implementation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excerpts instruct readers how the agency chose its baseline for impact estimates (referencing prior rule RIAs) and direct readers to earlier analyses for detailed methodology when special baselines are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public comment invitations specific to RIA/IRFA and responsiveness to new information
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies often reopen comment periods or specifically solicit comments on newly added RIA information or IRFA analyses; agencies may adjust the administrative record and respond to substantive comments on the RIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include reopening comment periods to invite comments on new cost/benefit figures, adding supporting information to the record, and explicitly requesting comment on the RIA/IRFA and related analyses (PRA, EO implementation).
